Issued at 333 PM CDT Sat Aug 22 2026

Currently...

The day started out on the wet side for a good chunk of the 
forecast area...as yet another upper level shortwave disturbance
(aided by increased lower-level convergence) made its way 
across the region...with a couple spots producing wind gusts 
around 60 MPH. That activity exited the area around mid-
morning...leaving behind a pretty nice day with plenty of sun. 
Upper air and satellite data showing continued northwesterly 
flow in place across the Central Plains this afternoon as the 
pattern remains well amplified across the CONUS. The main ridge 
axis extends north through the Rockies from high pressure 
centered mainly over CO/NM...sandwiched between areas of low 
pressure/southward extending troughing over northern Ontario and
just off the Pac NW coast. At the surface...a large area of 
high pressure is centered over near the ND/Canada border, with 
its axis extending south roughly along the MO River. This is 
keeping winds across the forecast area easterly, with speeds on 
the lighter side, around 10-15 MPH. No big surprises as far as 
temperatures go...with mid afternoon readings in the low-mid 
80s. 

This evening on into Sunday...

Quiet conditions this afternoon will continue on into the
evening hours, before precipitation chances ramp back up later
tonight. Off to our west...radar and satellite imagery showing 
scattered storms developing over the Rockies, as another 
shortwave disturbance rides around the edge of the ridge, and 
aided by east-southeasterly lower-level upslope flow. The main 
question as the late evening-overnight hours pass is how much of
this activity is sustained long enough to move into our 
forecast area. Kept the forecast dry through 06Z...and some of 
the hi-res models suggest it'd be even later than that by a few 
hours before activity creeps into our western edge. Aided by 
lift along an increased, but not overly strong, SSErly low level
jet...models are in pretty good agreement showing at least 
scattered activity making it into the forecast area. The timing 
may end up not too different than last night with the onset 
being around 09Z...but models suggest that activity lingers 
around the area longer, potentially not until early-mid 
afternoon before sliding off to our east. This activity is not 
expected to be severe...models still showing that while deeper 
layer shear isn't bad (30-35ish kts), the main axis of better 
instability focused just off to our west...so the SPC Day 1 
outlook areas remain both west and south of the area. 

Once the activity pushes east, the rest of the day Sunday is
dry, but will likely see more cloud cover linger longer into 
the day...especially across the eastern half of the area. This 
would impact high potential for the day...forecast currently has
mid 70s in the east to mid 80s in the west (where more sun is 
possible). Between the sfc high shifting more to our east and 
low pressure deepening over the High Plains...winds are expected
to turn more southerly for Sunday...with the potential for 
gusts near 20 MPH across areas mainly west of HWY 281. 

Later Sunday night into the overnight hours...little overall
change in the upper level pattern means there will the 
potential for yet another shortwave disturbance to bring 
additional storm chances to the area. Main difference during 
this period is that models still suggesting this disturbance 
tracks a bit further north (as does better convergence along the
LLJ)...and along with warmer mid-level temps the further SW you
go, result in these chances more of a glancing shot, focused 
across the NNErn third or so of the forecast area. Severe 
weather chances remain low through Sunday night- early Mon AM.

Monday and on...

Outside of any lingering activity early in the morning, the
daytime and at least early evening hours on Monday remain dry.
Models showing little movement in the location of the main 
upper level area high of high pressure and northward extending 
ridging into the Rockies...but do show that area of low pressure
currently off the Pac NW pushing further inland...sliding 
through the southern half of Saskatchewan during the daytime 
hours. Precipitation chances do return to the forecast late 
Monday night-Tuesday AM...but remain low (20-30 percent) as 
models vary with how much (if any?) activity impacts the 
forecast area, with the better upper level forcing well to our 
NW. 

Later Tuesday (more the evening/overnight hours) may bring
better thunderstorm chances to the area...as that main upper 
low is working its way more into MN, with the trough axis draped
further SW into the region. Storms may initially focus along an
accompanying sfc frontal boundary (though it's not a strong 
one)...later aided by an increasing LLJ. Still plenty of 
uncertainty and details to iron out...as being this far south of
